title: Nat Narain

cards: At a wedding, the dhol player picks up the pace, and before anyone decides to, feet are moving under the tables. Some music won't let a body sit still. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga this path hears in that key.
It's a short section, tucked in after the long, calm rooms of Ramkali, and its name is Nat Narain. So what does a lively raga do with devotion?

teach.b: Narain is a name for God, and here it's part of a raga's name. The hymns gathered under it belong to Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, and Guru Arjan, the fifth. The section opens with Guru Ram Das talking to his own mind.
In plain English, not word for word: my mind, repeat the Lord's Name day and night, and countless wrongs are set aside. He isn't lecturing a crowd.

He's turning to himself, the way you'd turn to a friend who keeps drifting off mid-conversation. That habit runs all through Gurbani: the mind gets spoken to directly, coaxed, encouraged, sometimes scolded.
In a lively raga, the coaxing has a bounce in its step.

The Granth gives devotion many moods, a raga for each, and one of them is lively. The same Name sung slow and heavy in one section comes back quick and bright in another. The raga sets the color; the Name stays the same.
In kirtan, the music carries the words; it doesn't cover them. A bright tune that buries the hymn has missed the point. A bright tune that gets a tired mind back on its feet has found it.

how: In kirtan, Sikh musicians sing the shabads of the Nat Narain section in that raga; the raga named at the head of a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the musical color it is sung in.

o: a long raga section of slow, solemn hymns
a festival dance done to the beat of a dhol
a short, lively raga of the Guru Granth Sahib

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.
p: carries the words, never covers them

s: devotion in the Granth is only ever slow and solemn
the Granth gives devotion many moods, a raga for each, and Nat Narain is a lively one.
the Nat Narain section opens with a Guru speaking to his own mind

games.q: you're a kirtan singer with a lively raga and a hymn about repeating the Name. what is the bright tune for?
o: carrying the words to a tired mind.
games.why: in kirtan the music serves the hymn. a bright tune that wakes a drifting mind up to the words has done its job.

practice: Sit up tall and, for a few breaths, breathe a little brisker than usual, the way you'd breathe walking up a short hill, or skip that part if it doesn't suit you. Then let the breath settle back to its own pace and stay with it.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each out-breath, the way Guru Ram Das turns to his mind, again and again; if you don't, count your out-breaths to ten and begin again.

wordCard.voice: Nat Narain. A short, lively raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Ram Das turns to his own mind and says: repeat the Name, day and night. Today's word.

orig.note: nat narain: the name of the raga at the head of this section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: lively. Sometimes a drifting mind just needs a friendly voice saying: come on, once more. Until tomorrow.
